details:
SunCity is a free web tool that shows whether the climate of any place on Earth is really changing, by how much, and how sure we are. You pick a place, and SunCity uses 45 years of NASA climate data (1981 to 2025) to calculate how much the temperature changes every ten years. It then tells you if that change is real or if there is not enough evidence yet. For example, nights in Mexicali are getting 0.53 °C warmer every ten years, and the result is real. In Hermosillo, the same calculation gives 0.21 °C every ten years, but there is not enough evidence yet.

We also built a second view that looks at Hermosillo sector by sector, at night, using NASA satellite data (MODIS and ECOSTRESS, from the International Space Station). This view uses test data for now, and the page says so clearly.

The benefit is simple: people, cities, and decision makers can see where the climate is changing and where to look first, without needing to be experts. SunCity does not cool the city. It points to where to look, and the action is human. Our goal is to start in Hermosillo, a city that reached 49.5 °C, and then work for any place on Earth.

What we used: HTML, CSS, and JavaScript with MapLibre GL for the maps; NASA POWER, MODIS, ECOSTRESS (through AppEEARS), and NASA GIBS map tiles; Python (numpy, scipy, pymannkendall, statsmodels) for the trend calculations; and population data from GPW v4.11. There is no database: the site is static and gets the data from NASA’s open services.

What makes it different and what we considered: we wrote the rules for deciding if a trend is real before calculating anything, so the tool says “not enough evidence yet” instead of promising something it cannot prove. We also chose to be open about limits: the sector view uses test data, and we do not claim to measure the effect of any measure on the city. We built it with two people, team 2A2G, and every number on the page comes from open data anyone can check.
